items.source_name: Mayo Clinic Laboratories — Specific Gravity, Random, Urine
items.locator: Clinical Information/Interpretation: increased urine specific gravity can occur with excessive body-water loss; decreased specific gravity can occur with diabetes insipidus. Interpret the result with clinical context rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.
items.version: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog entry; live reference rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs — Take Steps to Prevent Pressure Injuries: inspect skin regularly, reposition according to risk/condition, and use appropriate pressure-reducing/support surfaces such as special mattresses, overlays, or cushions when indicated.
items.version: Current VA Veterans Health Library pressure-injury prevention guidance; rechecked 2026-08-15.

options.A: Continue the standard mattress and rely on repositioning alone because support-surface selection does not affect pressure-injury prevention.
options.B: Reduce skin assessment frequency because repeated inspection increases friction and can worsen early sacral changes.
options.C: Stop routine repositioning after adding a cushion because a pressure-relieving device replaces the need for position changes.
options.D: Use an appropriate pressure-redistributing support surface while continuing individualized repositioning and regular skin assessment.

items.rationale: A high-risk client with early sacral skin changes needs a combined prevention approach. VA guidance supports regular skin inspection, repositioning, and appropriate support surfaces that reduce pressure. A support surface does not replace repositioning or surveillance, and a standard mattress should not be assumed adequate when skin changes are already emerging.

items.locator: FDA — Think It Through: Managing the Benefits and Risks of Medicines, ‘Know Your Medicines’: know what each medicine is for, when and how to take it, what to do for a missed dose, expected effects, important side effects/precautions, and relevant interactions.
items.version: Current FDA medication-safety consumer guidance at cited URL; rechecked 2026-08-15.

options.A: Review the brand name and purchase cost, then rely on the pharmacy label for the remaining instructions.
options.B: Review the medication's purpose, dose and schedule, important side effects and precautions, relevant interactions, and what to do if a dose is missed.
options.C: Review only the dose and administration time because discussing expected effects or adverse effects can reduce adherence.
options.D: Review the tablet's appearance and storage but omit missed-dose instructions because the response is the same for all medicines.

items.rationale: Safe medication self-management teaching includes why the medicine is used, dose and schedule, expected effects, important adverse effects and precautions, relevant interactions, and medication-specific instructions for missed doses. Option B is the only complete teaching plan. The other choices omit essential safety information or incorrectly imply that missed-dose instructions are universal.

items.locator: Using a Cane: a cane is appropriate when only a little help with balance/stability or one-sided weakness is needed; with substantial weakness or balance problems, crutches or a walker may be more appropriate. Among the listed options, a walker provides the broadest support for bilateral weakness.
items.version: MedlinePlus patient instruction reviewed 2025-04-01; current NLM resource rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: NIDDK — Treatment for Constipation: increase fiber, drink adequate liquids when appropriate, engage in regular physical activity, and establish healthy bowel habits/respond to the urge to defecate; stimulant laxatives are not the default first prevention measure.
items.version: Current NIDDK constipation guidance at cited federal URL; live content rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: CDC — How to Quit Smoking / Quitlines: 1-800-QUIT-NOW connects callers to free, confidential quitline coaching and cessation support; counseling and cessation medications improve quit success.
items.version: Current CDC tobacco-cessation guidance; quitline information updated/rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: CDC — Tips to Support Healthy Routines for Children and Teens: support nutritious eating patterns, water/healthier beverages, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and reasonable limits on recreational screen time as family routines.

HHS Administration for Community Living — What If I Suspect Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation?: Adult Protective Services is the principal public agency responding to reports of abuse/neglect/exploitation of vulnerable adults; use emergency/law-enforcement channels when immediate danger exists. Reporting duties vary by state law.
items.version: ACL page modified 2026-03-18; current federal elder-justice guidance rechecked 2026-08-15. Mandatory-reporting duties must be applied under current jurisdiction law/policy.

options.A: Wait for medical confirmation of physical injury before reporting because suspicion alone is not enough to contact protective services.
options.B: Keep suspected financial exploitation or neglect within the family unless the older adult specifically requests a formal report.
options.C: Recognize physical, emotional, sexual, financial, and neglect-related abuse and follow current state law and policy for reporting to APS or emergency/law-enforcement services as appropriate.
options.D: Limit reporting to licensed clinicians because family members and community workers cannot contact Adult Protective Services about suspected maltreatment.

items.rationale: Elder maltreatment can include physical, emotional, sexual, financial, and neglect-related harm. ACL identifies Adult Protective Services as a principal response agency and directs emergency action when immediate danger exists. For nursing practice, the exact mandatory-reporting duty must follow current state law and organizational policy; therefore option C is accurate without falsely imposing one universal reporting procedure on every jurisdiction.

items.locator: NIMH — Schizophrenia, Symptoms: psychotic symptoms include hallucinations, delusions, and thought disorder; negative symptoms and cognitive symptoms are separate categories.
items.version: NIMH Schizophrenia publication revised 2024 and current in 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.

options.A: They are symptoms unrelated to schizophrenia because hallucinations and fixed false beliefs occur only in mood or neurologic disorders.
options.B: They are psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia: hearing voices is a hallucination and fixed coded-message beliefs are delusional beliefs.
options.C: They are exclusively cognitive symptoms because hallucinations and delusions primarily reflect deficits in attention, memory, and executive function.
options.D: They are negative symptoms because hallucinations and delusions represent reductions in motivation, emotional expression, speech, and social engagement.

items.rationale: NIMH classifies hallucinations and delusions as psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia. Hearing voices is an auditory hallucination, and a fixed belief that strangers are sending coded television messages is delusional. Negative symptoms involve reductions such as diminished motivation or emotional expression; cognitive symptoms involve functions such as attention and memory.

items.locator: NIMH — Bipolar Disorder, Manic Episode symptoms: elevated or irritable mood with increased activity/energy, decreased need for sleep, rapid/pressured speech, racing thoughts, and unusually high energy/activity.
items.version: NIMH Bipolar Disorder publication revised 2025 and current in 2026; rechecked 2026-08-15.
